structures.summary: The lateral pterygoid is a short, thick chewing muscle with superior and inferior heads. They arise from the greater wing of the sphenoid and the lateral pterygoid plate and run backward to the neck of the mandible and the jaw joint disc and capsule.
structures.function: It pulls the jaw forward and helps open the mouth; acting on one side, it swings the jaw to the opposite side.
structures.location: It lies deep in the infratemporal fossa, above the medial pterygoid and in front of the jaw joint.
facts: It is the only muscle of mastication that helps open the mouth.
It is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

structures.summary: Six muscles move each eyeball: four recti (superior, inferior, medial and lateral) that arise from the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit, and two obliques. A seventh, levator palpebrae superioris, raises the upper eyelid. The superior oblique tendon passes through a fibrous pulley, the trochlea.
structures.function: They turn the eye up, down, in and out and rotate it, keeping both eyes aligned on the same target.
structures.location: They lie within the bony orbit around the eyeball.
facts: Nerve supply follows the formula LR6 SO4: lateral rectus by the abducens nerve (VI), superior oblique by the trochlear nerve (IV) and all the rest by the oculomotor nerve (III).
A third-nerve palsy causes a drooping eyelid because levator palpebrae superioris is paralysed.

structures.summary: The platysma is a broad, thin sheet of muscle in the skin of the front of the neck. It runs from the fascia over the upper chest and shoulder up over the collarbone to the lower jaw and the skin of the lower face.
structures.function: It tenses the skin of the neck and pulls down the corners of the mouth and the lower jaw, as in an expression of strain or horror.
structures.location: It lies just under the skin of the front and sides of the neck.
facts: It is supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), like the other muscles of facial expression.
Its vertical bands become more visible with age.

structures.summary: The buccinator is a thin, four-sided muscle that forms the muscular wall of the cheek. It arises from the outer surfaces of the upper and lower jaws near the molars and from the pterygomandibular raphe and blends into the lips at the corner of the mouth. (The model spells it 'Bucinator'.)
structures.function: It presses the cheek against the teeth, keeping food between the teeth during chewing, and helps blow air out, as when playing a trumpet.
structures.location: It lies deep in the cheek, between the upper and lower jaws; the parotid duct pierces it opposite the upper second molar.
facts: Its name comes from the Latin buccinator, 'trumpeter'.
It is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, not the buccal branch of the trigeminal nerve, which only carries sensation.

structures.summary: The zygomaticus major and minor are slender muscles running from the cheekbone (zygomatic bone) down to the mouth. The major goes to the corner of the mouth (modiolus) and the minor to the upper lip.
structures.function: Zygomaticus major pulls the corner of the mouth up and out in smiling; zygomaticus minor lifts the upper lip.
structures.location: They cross the cheek diagonally from the cheekbone toward the corner of the mouth.
facts: A true (Duchenne) smile combines zygomaticus major with contraction of orbicularis oculi around the eye.
Both are supplied by the zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve.

structures.medical: Levator labii superioris, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi and levator anguli oris
structures.summary: These muscles run from the upper jaw and the area below the eye down into the upper lip. Levator labii superioris lifts the lip, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (listed in the model as 'Levator nasolabialis') also reaches the side of the nose, and levator anguli oris goes to the corner of the mouth.
structures.function: They raise the upper lip and the corners of the mouth, as in sneering or smiling, and one flares the nostril.
structures.location: They lie in the upper cheek between the lower edge of the orbit and the upper lip.
facts: They help shape the nasolabial fold, the crease running from the nose to the corner of the mouth.
All are supplied by the facial nerve.

structures.medical: Depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris and mentalis
structures.summary: These muscles arise from the lower jaw below the mouth. Depressor anguli oris pulls on the corner of the mouth, depressor labii inferioris on the lower lip, and mentalis on the skin of the chin.
structures.function: They pull the corners of the mouth and the lower lip down, as in frowning or sadness; mentalis raises and wrinkles the chin and pushes out the lower lip, as in pouting.
structures.location: They lie on the front of the lower jaw below the lower lip.
facts: They are supplied by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve; injury to this branch causes an uneven smile.
Mentalis produces the dimpled 'orange peel' look of the chin in some people.

structures.summary: The risorius is a thin, narrow band of muscle running horizontally across the cheek to the corner of the mouth. It arises from the fascia over the parotid gland and masseter.
structures.function: It pulls the corner of the mouth sideways, as in a grin or a grimace.
structures.location: It lies in the lower cheek, between the masseter and the corner of the mouth.
facts: It is very variable and sometimes absent.
It is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve.

structures.medical: Nasalis, depressor septi nasi, procerus and corrugator supercilii
structures.summary: Several small facial muscles act on the nose and brow. Nasalis compresses or flares the nostrils, depressor septi nasi pulls down the nasal septum, procerus lies over the bridge of the nose, and corrugator supercilii runs from the inner end of the eyebrow ridge into the skin of the eyebrow.
structures.function: They move the nostrils and the skin of the nose and brow; procerus makes horizontal lines across the nose bridge and corrugator draws the eyebrows together in frowning.
structures.location: They lie over the nose and between the eyebrows.
facts: The vertical frown lines between the eyebrows come mainly from corrugator supercilii, and are a common target of cosmetic botulinum toxin injections.
All are supplied by the facial nerve.

structures.summary: The temporoparietalis is a thin, variable sheet of muscle on the side of the scalp above the ear. It lies between the frontal belly of occipitofrontalis and the ear muscles and blends into the epicranial aponeurosis.
structures.function: It helps tighten the scalp and may raise the ears slightly.
structures.location: It lies on the side of the head above and in front of the ear, over the temporal fascia.
facts: Together with occipitofrontalis it is grouped as the epicranius muscle.
It is supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve.
